cse-2013-cs-1.approach: Check commutativity by swapping operands and associativity by expanding both bracketings with a counterexample.

steps.title: Commutative
steps.body: $x \oplus y = x^2 + y^2 = y^2 + x^2 = y \oplus x$ for all integers, so $\oplus$ is commutative.

steps.title: Associative?
steps.body:
$(x \oplus y) \oplus z = (x^2+y^2)^2 + z^2$ while $x \oplus (y \oplus z) = x^2 + (y^2+z^2)^2$.

Take $x=1, y=0, z=0$: left $= (1+0)^2 + 0 = 1$; right $= 1 + (0+0)^2 = 1$ — equal, so try $x=1,y=1,z=0$: left $= (1+1)^2 + 0 = 4$; right $= 1 + (1+0)^2 = 2$. Since $4 \ne 2$, $\oplus$ is not associative.

optionAnalysis.reason: Correct: symmetric in $x,y$, but $(1\oplus1)\oplus0 = 4 \ne 2 = 1\oplus(1\oplus0)$.
Fails associativity (counterexample above).
It is commutative and not associative — both parts wrong.
It is commutative.

pitfalls: Testing associativity only with zeros, where both sides happen to agree.
cse-2013-cs-1.verification: Another check: $x=y=z=1$ gives $(2)^2+1 = 5$ vs $1+(2)^2 = 5$ (equal), but $x=2,y=z=1$ gives $(5)^2+1=26$ vs $4+(2)^2=8$ — confirms non-associativity.

cse-2013-cs-3.approach: Reduce each option to the given Vandermonde determinant with elementary row/column operations; the one that only reaches the original up to a column swap (sign change) is the odd one out.

steps.title: Option A
steps.body:
Columns $C_1=1$, $C_2 = x(x+1) = x^2+x$, $C_3 = x+1$.

$C_3 \to C_3 - C_1$ gives $x$; then $C_2 \to C_2 - C_3$ gives $x^2 + x - x = x^2$. Now the columns are $(1,\ x^2,\ x)$ — the original with $C_2, C_3$ swapped, so
$$\det(A) = -\begin{vmatrix}1&x&x^2\\1&y&y^2\\1&z&z^2\end{vmatrix}.$$
It is NOT equal (unless the determinant is 0).

steps.title: Option B
steps.body: $C_2 \to C_2 - C_1$ gives $x$, $C_3 \to C_3 - C_1$ gives $x^2$: exactly the original. Equal.

steps.title: Options C and D
steps.body:
C: rows are $R_1 - R_2$, $R_2 - R_3$, $R_3$ of the original; adding $R_3$ back to row 2 and then the new row 2 to row 1 undoes it — such operations keep the determinant. Equal.

D: rows are $R_1 + R_2$, $R_2 + R_3$, $R_3$. $\det(R_1+R_2, R_2+R_3, R_3) = \det(R_1+R_2, R_2, R_3) = \det(R_1, R_2, R_3)$. Equal.

answer.value: Option (A) — it equals $-1$ times the given determinant
answer.keyNote: The stored key D is wrong: D is obtained from the original by adding rows (R1+R2, R2+R3, R3), which leaves the determinant unchanged, whereas A reduces to the original with two columns swapped, i.e. its negative.

optionAnalysis.reason: Correct: $C_3-C_1$ then $C_2-C_3$ yields columns $1, x^2, x$ — a column swap, so the value is negated.
$C_2-C_1$, $C_3-C_1$ give back $1, x, x^2$ exactly — equal.
Rows are differences of consecutive original rows plus the last row — row-addition operations, equal.
Rows $R_1+R_2$, $R_2+R_3$, $R_3$ — row-addition operations, equal. (Stored key, but it is equal, not unequal.)

pitfalls: Forgetting that swapping two columns flips the sign.
Thinking a row like $(2, x+y, dots)$ scales the determinant — it is a sum of rows, not a multiple.

cse-2013-cs-9.approach: Each reduction corresponds to one internal node of the parse tree; with every right side of length at least 2, a tree with n leaves has at most n−1 internal nodes.

steps.title: Reductions = internal nodes
steps.body: A bottom-up parser performs exactly one reduce move per internal (non-terminal) node of the parse tree.

steps.title: Bound the internal nodes
steps.body: With no $\epsilon$-productions and no productions with a single symbol on the right, every internal node has at least 2 children. A tree with $n$ leaves and every internal node of degree $\ge 2$ has at most $n-1$ internal nodes (each reduction replaces $\ge 2$ symbols by 1, shrinking the sentential form by $\ge 1$, from $n$ symbols down to 1).

steps.title: Maximum
steps.body: Hence at most $n-1$ reduce moves, achieved when every production has exactly two symbols on the right (e.g. $S \to SS \mid ab$-style binary trees).

cse-2013-cs-10.approach: Priority grows with waiting time; the running process stops waiting, so at each T-boundary the longest-waiting process is picked — this rotates through processes like round-robin with quantum T.

steps.title: Dynamics
steps.body: All start at priority 0 at time 0. Whoever runs during an interval of length $T$ does not wait, so its priority stays behind; every other process's priority grows. At the next re-evaluation the process that has waited longest has the highest priority and is scheduled.

steps.title: Result
steps.body: Each process runs for $T$ units in turn and goes to the back of the "waiting longest" order — exactly round-robin with time quantum $T$.

optionAnalysis.reason: FCFS never preempts; here the running job is preempted after T when others have waited longer.
Correct: the longest-waiting process gets the next slice of T — round-robin order.
Burst lengths play no role in the priority, so it cannot be SJF.
SRTF needs remaining burst times, which this scheduler never uses.

pitfalls: Choosing FCFS because priority depends on arrival — waiting time keeps changing after preemption.
cse-2013-cs-10.verification: Three processes P1, P2, P3: P1 runs [0,T); at T, P2 and P3 have waited T, P1 has waited 0 → P2 (tie broken by order); at 2T, P3 has waited 2T → P3; then P1 (waited 2T) — cyclic order P1, P2, P3, P1, …
